## Transcript [...] # Meet Fompi: your personal security & privacy companion

Most of the internet is exactly what it says it is. Fompi is for the rest.

It sits quietly in your browser and speaks up when something is off, in plain words:
a sign-in page on an address that only looks like the real one
a "verify you are human" page that wants a command pasted into your computer
a phishing email in Gmail or Outlook
a download in disguise, like invoice.pdf.exe
an AI notetaker joining your call in Meet, Teams or Zoom
a fake virus warning with a phone number

Fompi Pro also keeps card numbers, IDs, passwords and API keys out of AI chats, by swapping them for placeholders before they are sent. [...] ## Transcript

Most of the internet is exactly what it says it is. Most this page says it is your company login. The address disagrees. Fmpy noticed. This is you about to hand an AI your card number. FPY swaps it for a placeholder. [snorts and clears throat] The AI will cope. This email is from PayPal. Sure it is. And this is a stranger called Notetaker joining your call. Fmpy mentions it. Someone should. A fake verification. an invoice that is secretly a program, a virus warning with a phone number. Fmpy has opinions on your Mac. It also keeps an eye on what you copy, what you download, and who is using your microphone. Every check runs on your device. It tells no one, and it stays quiet until something is off. Fompy, your personal security and privacy companion.

results.title: Why do companion apps create higher privacy and legal risk than standalone mobile apps?
results.content:
When sensitive signals or personal data move across service boundaries, teams should also verify that the legal basis and the technical implementation match. A disclosure that names generic telemetry is not enough if the app is actually collecting precise behavioral data or forwarding it to partners. The gap between expected use and actual use is where privacy complaints, regulator scrutiny, and consumer trust failures usually start. [...] ## Risk and Threat Considerations

Companion apps are attractive to adversaries and regulators for the same reason: they can sit on a rich data path and observe behavior at scale. If the app overcollects, transmits too broadly, or stores identifiable signals without clear purpose limits, the exposure can include privacy violations, unauthorized interception arguments, consumer protection claims, and broader compliance findings.

Failure mechanism: The companion design creates a broader collection and transmission layer than the user expects, so sensitive signals can be inferred, retained, or shared even when no single screen appears invasive. [...] ← Back to all FAQ

Companion apps often sit between users, devices, and external services, so they can collect more sensitive signals than expected. Audio selections, usage data, location, and account metadata can reveal personal traits or habits, which raises privacy, wiretap, and consumer protection concerns. The risk grows when data collection is not clearly disclosed, not necessary for service delivery, or transmitted to third parties.
